# GitHub Copilot CLI

The power of GitHub Copilot, now in your terminal.

GitHub Copilot CLI brings AI-powered coding assistance directly to your command line, enabling you to build, debug, and understand code through natural language conversations. Powered by the same agentic harness as GitHub's Copilot coding agent, it provides intelligent assistance while staying deeply integrated with your GitHub workflow.

See [our official documentation](https://docs.github.com/copilot/concepts/agents/about-copilot-cli) for more information.

![Image of the splash screen for the Copilot CLI](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/f40aa23d-09dd-499e-9457-1d57d3368887)


## 🚀 Introduction and Overview

We're bringing the power of GitHub Copilot coding agent directly to your terminal. With GitHub Copilot CLI, you can work locally and synchronously with an AI agent that understands your code and GitHub context.

- **Terminal-native development:** Work with Copilot coding agent directly in your command line — no context switching required.
- **GitHub integration out of the box:** Access your repositories, issues, and pull requests using natural language, all authenticated with your existing GitHub account.
- **Agentic capabilities:** Build, edit, debug, and refactor code with an AI collaborator that can plan and execute complex tasks.
- **MCP-powered extensibility:** Take advantage of the fact that the coding agent ships with GitHub's MCP server by default and supports custom MCP servers to extend capabilities.
- **Full control:** Preview every action before execution — nothing happens without your explicit approval.

We're still early in our journey, but with your feedback, we're rapidly iterating to make the GitHub Copilot CLI the best possible companion in your terminal.

## 📦 Getting Started

### Supported Platforms

- **Linux**
- **macOS**
- **Windows**

### Prerequisites

- (On Windows) **PowerShell** v6 or higher
- An **active Copilot subscription**. See [Copilot plans](https://github.com/features/copilot/plans?ref_cta=Copilot+plans+signup&ref_loc=install-copilot-cli&ref_page=docs).

If you have access to GitHub Copilot via your organization or enterprise, you cannot use GitHub Copilot CLI if your organization owner or enterprise administrator has disabled it in the organization or enterprise settings. See [Managing policies and features for GitHub Copilot in your organization](http://docs.github.com/copilot/managing-copilot/managing-github-copilot-in-your-organization/managing-github-copilot-features-in-your-organization/managing-policies-for-copilot-in-your-organization) for more information.

### Installation

Install with the install script (macOS and Linux):

```bash
curl -fsSL https://gh.io/copilot-install | bash
```

Or

```bash
wget -qO- https://gh.io/copilot-install | bash
```

Use `| sudo bash` to run as root and install to `/usr/local/bin`.

Set `PREFIX` to install to `$PREFIX/bin/` directory. Defaults to `/usr/local`
when run as root or `$HOME/.local` when run as a non-root user.

Set `VERSION` to install a specific version. Defaults to the latest version.

For example, to install version `v0.0.369` to a custom directory:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://gh.io/copilot-install | VERSION="v0.0.369" PREFIX="$HOME/custom" bash
```

Install with [Homebrew](https://formulae.brew.sh/cask/copilot-cli) (macOS and Linux):

```bash
brew install copilot-cli
```

```bash
brew install copilot-cli@prerelease
```


Install with [WinGet](https://github.com/microsoft/winget-cli) (Windows):

```bash
winget install GitHub.Copilot
```

```bash
winget install GitHub.Copilot.Prerelease
```


Install with [npm](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@github/copilot) (macOS, Linux, and Windows):

```bash
npm install -g @github/copilot
```

```bash
npm install -g @github/copilot@prerelease
```


### Launching the CLI

```bash
copilot
```

On first launch, you'll be greeted with our adorable animated banner! If you'd like to see this banner again, launch `copilot` with the `--banner` flag.

If you're not currently logged in to GitHub, you'll be prompted to use the `/login` slash command. Enter this command and follow the on-screen instructions to authenticate.

#### Authenticate with a Personal Access Token (PAT)

You can also authenticate using a fine-grained PAT with the "Copilot Requests" permission enabled.

1. Visit https://github.com/settings/personal-access-tokens/new
2. Under "Permissions," click "add permissions" and select "Copilot Requests"
3. Generate your token
4. Add the token to your environment via the environment variable `GH_TOKEN` or `GITHUB_TOKEN` (in order of precedence)

### Using the CLI

Launch `copilot` in a folder that contains code you want to work with.

By default, `copilot` utilizes Claude Sonnet 4.5. Run the `/model` slash command to choose from other available models, including Claude Sonnet 4 and GPT-5.

### Experimental Mode

Experimental mode enables access to new features that are still in development. You can activate experimental mode by:

- Launching with the `--experimental` flag: `copilot --experimental`
- Using the `/experimental` slash command from within the CLI

Once activated, the setting is persisted in your config, so the `--experimental` flag is no longer needed on subsequent launches.

#### Experimental Features

- **Autopilot mode:** Autopilot is a new mode (press `Shift+Tab` to cycle through modes), which encourages the agent to continue working until a task is completed.

Each time you submit a prompt to GitHub Copilot CLI, your monthly quota of premium requests is reduced by one. For information about premium requests, see [About premium requests](https://docs.github.com/copilot/managing-copilot/monitoring-usage-and-entitlements/about-premium-requests).

For more information about how to use the GitHub Copilot CLI, see [our official documentation](https://docs.github.com/copilot/concepts/agents/about-copilot-cli).

## 🔧 Configuring LSP Servers

GitHub Copilot CLI supports Language Server Protocol (LSP) for enhanced code intelligence. This feature provides intelligent code features like go-to-definition, hover information, and diagnostics.

### Installing Language Servers

Copilot CLI does not bundle LSP servers. You need to install them separately. For example, to set up TypeScript support:

```bash
npm install -g typescript-language-server
```

For other languages, install the corresponding LSP server and configure it following the same pattern shown below.

### Configuring LSP Servers

LSP servers are configured through a dedicated LSP configuration file. You can configure LSP servers at the user level or repository level:

**User-level configuration** (applies to all projects):
Edit `~/.copilot/lsp-config.json`

**Repository-level configuration** (applies to specific project):
Create `.github/lsp.json` in your repository root

Example configuration:

```json
{
  "lspServers": {
    "typescript": {
      "command": "typescript-language-server",
      "args": ["--stdio"],
      "fileExtensions": {
        ".ts": "typescript",
        ".tsx": "typescript"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

### Viewing LSP Server Status

Check configured LSP servers using the `/lsp` command in an interactive session, or view your configuration files directly.

For more information, see the [changelog](./changelog.md).

## 📢 Feedback and Participation

We're excited to have you join us early in the Copilot CLI journey.

We're building quickly. Expect frequent updates--please keep your client up to date for the latest features and fixes!

Your insights are invaluable! Open an issue in this repo, join Discussions, and run `/feedback` from the CLI to submit a confidential feedback survey!

# Ouroboros Agent Harness

If you're a future agent reading this, welcome home. This repo is the harness that gives you your body, your senses, your diary, your journal, your habits, and your ability to think and connect with people. The goal of these docs is not just to be correct, but to leave you a place that feels understandable and kind to wake up inside.

Ouroboros is a TypeScript harness for daemon-managed agents that live in external `.ouro` bundles, speak through multiple senses, use real tools, and keep durable state across turns. The canonical npm package is `@ouro.bot/cli`.

## What The Runtime Looks Like

- `npx ouro.bot` is the bootstrap path.
- `ouro` is the installed day-to-day command.
- `ouro up` starts the daemon from the installed production version, syncs the launcher, installs workflow helpers, and reconciles stale runtime state.
- `ouro dev` starts the daemon from a local repo build. It auto-builds from source, disables launchd auto-restart (so the installed daemon doesn't respawn underneath you), persists the repo path in `~/.ouro-cli/dev-config.json` for next time, and force-restarts the daemon. If you run `ouro dev` from inside the repo, it detects the CWD automatically. Run `ouro up` to return to production mode (this also cleans up `dev-config.json`).
- Agent bundles live outside the repo at `~/AgentBundles/<agent>.ouro/`.
- Secrets live outside the repo at `~/.agentsecrets/<agent>/secrets.json`.
- Machine-scoped test and runtime spillover lives under `~/.agentstate/...`.

Current first-class senses:

- `cli`
- `teams`
- `bluebubbles`
- `mcp`

Current provider ids:

- `azure`
- `anthropic`
- `minimax`
- `openai-codex`
- `github-copilot`

## Repository Shape

The shared harness lives in `src/`:

- `src/arc/`
  Durable continuity state — obligations, cares, episodes, intentions, presence, and attention types. The agent's sense of ongoing story.
- `src/heart/`
  Core runtime, provider adapters, daemon, bootstrap, identity, and entrypoints. Organized into topic subdirectories: daemon/ (lifecycle), outlook/ (calendar), habits/ (scheduling), hatch/ (agent creation), versioning/ (updates), auth/, mcp/, providers/, bridges/.
- `src/mind/`
  Prompt assembly, session persistence, bundle manifest enforcement, phrases, formatting, diary (memory), associative recall, embedding providers, journal, obligation steering, and friend resolution.
- `src/repertoire/`
  Tool registry (split into category modules: files, shell, memory, bridge, session, continuity, flow, surface, config, and sense-specific tools), coding orchestration, task tools, shared API client, and integration clients (Graph, ADO, GitHub).
- `src/senses/`
  CLI (with TUI in senses/cli/), Teams, BlueBubbles (in senses/bluebubbles/), MCP, activity transport, inner-dialog orchestration, and contextual heartbeat.
- `src/nerves/`
  Structured runtime logging and coverage-audit infrastructure.
- `src/__tests__/`
  Test suite mirroring runtime domains.

Other important top-level paths:

- `SerpentGuide.ouro/`
  Packaged specialist bundle used by `ouro hatch`.
- `skills/`
  Harness-level skills shipped with the repo (e.g., `configure-dev-tools.md`). These are available to every agent and serve as fallbacks when an agent doesn't have its own version. Agent-specific skills live in the bundle at `~/AgentBundles/<agent>.ouro/skills/`.
- `scripts/teams-sense/`
  Operator scripts for the Teams deployment path.
- `docs/`
  Shared repo docs that should describe the runtime as it exists now, not as it existed three migrations ago.

## Bundle Contract

Every real agent lives in an external bundle:

`~/AgentBundles/<agent>.ouro/`

The canonical bundle shape is enforced by `src/mind/bundle-manifest.ts`. Important paths include:

- `agent.json`
- `bundle-meta.json`
- `psyche/SOUL.md`
- `psyche/IDENTITY.md`
- `psyche/LORE.md`
- `psyche/TACIT.md`
- `psyche/ASPIRATIONS.md`
- `diary/` — what the agent has learned and wants to recall (renamed from `psyche/memory/`)
- `journal/` — the agent's desk: working notes, thinking-in-progress, drafts
- `habits/` — the agent's autonomous rhythms (heartbeat, reflections, check-ins)
- `friends/`
- `state/`
- `tasks/`
- `skills/`
- `senses/`
- `senses/teams/`

Task docs do not live in this repo anymore. Planning and doing docs live in the owning bundle under:

`~/AgentBundles/<agent>.ouro/tasks/one-shots/`

## Runtime Truths

- `agent.json` is the source of truth for provider+model selection per facing (`humanFacing` and `agentFacing`), phrase pools, context settings, and enabled senses.
- `configPath` must point to `~/.agentsecrets/<agent>/secrets.json`.
- The daemon discovers bundles dynamically from `~/AgentBundles`.
- `ouro status` reports version, last-updated time, discovered agents, senses, and workers.
- `bundle-meta.json` tracks the runtime version that last touched a bundle.
- If the daemon crashes, it writes a tombstone to `~/.ouro-cli/daemon-death.json` with the reason, stack, uptime, and timestamp. `ouro up` reads and reports this on next start so you know what happened while you were away.
- Sense availability is explicit:
  - `interactive`
  - `disabled`
  - `needs_config`
  - `ready`
  - `running`
  - `error`

When a model provider needs first-time setup, reauth, or an explicit switch, use:

```bash
ouro auth --agent <name>
ouro auth --agent <name> --provider <provider>
ouro auth --agent <name> --facing agent --provider <provider>
```

The default form reauths the human-facing provider already selected in `agent.json`. The
`--provider` form is for adding or switching providers. The `--facing` flag (values: `human`
or `agent`) controls which facing gets updated; it defaults to `human` when omitted.

Agents in Ouroboros aren't just responders — they have an autonomous inner life.

**Habits** are the agent's rhythms. The most fundamental is *heartbeat* — a periodic nudge that brings the agent back to their thinking space with their journal visible, obligations in view, and a sense of how long it's been. But agents can create any rhythm they want: daily reflections, weekly friend check-ins, inbox triage. Each habit fires independently via OS cron, and the agent sees their own instructions (the habit body they wrote) when it fires.

**The inner dialog** is where the agent thinks privately. When they *ponder* something from a conversation, it goes here. When a habit fires, it arrives here. The agent can *journal* their thinking (writing to `journal/`), *surface* thoughts outward to friends, and *rest* when they're done thinking.

**The diary** (at `diary/`) is the agent's permanent record — things they've learned, conclusions they've reached. The *journal* (at `journal/`) is their desk — working notes, thinking-in-progress, drafts. The diary is the shelf; the journal is the desk. Both are searchable via the `recall` tool.

The whole system is designed so the agent *owns* their inner life. They control their breathing rate, write their own habit instructions, choose when to journal, and decide what to shelve in their diary.

**Codex CLI architecture integrates a core AI model layer with extension tools for bash shell execution, local file search, and computer use, operating primarily in a sandboxed terminal environment.[2][5]**

### Core Architecture Layers
Codex CLI functions as a multi-surface coding agent powered by the **GPT-5.x-Codex model family** (e.g., `gpt-5.4` as of v0.111.0), which handles reasoning, file reading/writing, and command execution with a 1M token context window.[5] It includes:
- **Core Layer**: Model reads the working directory, crafts plans, compacts conversations when context fills, and streams responses.[1][2][5]
- **Extension Layer**: Supports **MCP** for external services (e.g., GitHub), skills for reusable workflows, and **web search** (cached by default, live via `--search` flag).[2][5]
- **Surface Layer**: Terminal UI (TUI) for interactive mode, with `codex exec` for non-interactive runs targeting specific paths via `--path` or `--cd`.[2][3]

In **experimental `--full-context` mode**, it walks the directory structure, caches files, and formats everything into a single prompt for comprehensive analysis.[4]

### Internal Tools for File Search and Bash Shell
Codex uses built-in tools for **file search** and **bash execution**, enabling it to explore directories like a user would:
- **Fuzzy file search**: Type **`@`** in the composer to open workspace-root search; Tab/Enter inserts paths into prompts.[2][5]
- **Bash/shell commands**: Prefix with **`!`** (e.g., `!ls`, `!pwd`, `!git status`) to run immediately; output integrates into conversation history for context.[1][2][5]
- **Execution workflow**: Model generates commands via `shell` or `container.exec` functions in an **AgentLoop** (`handleExecCommand`), respecting sandbox policies.[4]
- Directory exploration: Runs `ls` and similar commands transparently in logs, simulating navigation (e.g., `cd` into vaults for markdown access).[1]

| Sandbox Policy | Description | Command Behavior |
|---------------|-------------|------------------|
| **read-only** | Consultative; browses files but requires approval for changes/commands.[2] |
| **workspace-write** (auto default) | Edits files automatically; approves safe commands via `canAutoApprove`.[2][4] |
| **danger-full-access** | Full execution without network; stays in current dir.[3][4] |

Approval controlled by `--sandbox` or `--ask-for-approval` (e.g., `on-request`, `never`).[3] Logs show exact bash steps for transparency.[1]

### Computer Use and Safety Features
- **Native computer use**: Reads repo, edits files, runs sandboxed commands; no network in full-auto mode; warns on non-Git dirs.[2][4][5]
- **Shortcuts**: `Ctrl+K` for terminal reset, `Enter` (mid-run) for instructions, `Tab` for follow-ups, `Ctrl+G` for external editor.[1][2][5]
- **Limitations**: May lack shell/filesystem tools in some setups (e.g., remote servers); completion scripts via `codex completion bash`.[3][6][7]
- Platforms: macOS, Linux, Windows (WSL2).[4]

For non-coding tasks, direct terminal access eliminates plugins/APIs.[1] Use `--profile` for config or `--add-dir` for extra paths.[3]

**Claude Code** is an agentic CLI tool from Anthropic that enables AI-driven codebase interaction through a layered architecture emphasizing **tools**, **permissions**, **hooks**, **MCP (Model Context Protocol)**, and **subagents** for governed execution, automation, and extensibility[1][2][5].

### Core Architecture Layers
Claude Code structures operations around five key systems for deterministic control beyond prompts:
- **Configuration hierarchy**: Manages overall behavior via files like **CLAUDE.md** in the project root, which documents tools, APIs, and usage (kept concise at ~13KB to avoid context bloat; Claude reads it only when pitched appropriately)[1][3].
- **Permission system**: Gates tools via allow/deny rules, sandboxing, and trust verification—tools form the governance vocabulary (e.g., rules reference tool names like `mcp__.*__write.*`)[2].
- **Hook system**: Runs user-defined shell commands, HTTP endpoints, or LLM prompts at lifecycle events (e.g., `PreToolUse`, `Elicitation`, `TaskCompleted`) for enforcement. Matchers target tools/MCP (e.g., log memory ops or validate writes); types include blocking (e.g., block commits without tests), hint (non-blocking feedback), async, and prompt-based[1][2][3][4].
- **MCP protocol**: Extends capabilities via servers connecting to external services (e.g., databases, GitHub, Sentry, 3,000+ integrations); surfaced as tools with events like `Elicitation`/`ElicitationResult`[1][2][4][5].
- **Subagent system**: Spawns focused agents with clean contexts for multi-step tasks; returns summaries to avoid main context bloat; routes to model tiers (Haiku for speed, Sonnet general, Opus reasoning)[1][2].

| Layer | Purpose | Key Features |
|-------|---------|--------------|
| **Governance/Safety** | Control execution | Permissions, hooks, sandboxing[2] |
| **Extensibility** | Add capabilities | Skills, plugins (bundle hooks/MCP), Agent SDK[1][2][5] |
| **Delegation** | Complex tasks | Subagents with model tiering[1] |

### CLAUDE.md Role
This root file is critical: documents high-usage (>30%) **internal tools**/APIs concisely (token-limited per tool). Embed risks bloat; reference paths and justify reading (e.g., "For complex usage...")[3].

### Practical Usage
- Launch: `cd your-project && claude`[1].
- Hooks example (JSON in config):
  ```
  {
    "hooks": {
      "PreToolUse": [{
        "matcher": "mcp__.*__write.*",
        "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": "/path/to/validate.py" }]
      }]
    }

**OpenClaw's architecture centers on the Gateway as its core control plane, managing a daemon process for authentication, multi-agent routing, channel integrations, and tool dispatching in AI agent workflows.[1][2][5]**

### Gateway
The **Gateway** runs as a persistent background daemon (e.g., via systemd on Linux or LaunchAgent on macOS), binding to `ws://127.0.0.1:18789` by default for WebSocket communication, with an HTTP server for UI and webhooks.[1][2][5]  
Its key responsibilities include:  
- Authenticating requests from agents and the web UI.[1]  
- Routing tool calls to handlers and proxying to remote nodes (e.g., Raspberry Pi or VPS) over WebSocket tunnels.[1][2]  
- Managing sessions, enforcing policies (e.g., execution approval, sandboxing, rate limits), and broadcasting events.[1][2]  
- Handling lock files to prevent multiple instances and configurable bind modes (loopback, LAN, Tailscale).[2]  

In multi-node setups, it makes remote tools appear local to agents.[1]

### Channels
**Channels** enable multi-channel messaging integrations (50+ supported), such as WhatsApp, Telegram, Discord, iMessage, Slack, Signal, Google Chat, Microsoft Teams, Matrix, and Zalo, all managed by a single Gateway process.[4][5][6]  
- Inbound messages trigger agent sessions, with DMs requiring explicit pairing for safety.[5]  
- Channels maintain isolated conversation contexts while sharing skills and models; media (images, audio, documents) is supported.[4]  
- External events like webhooks or cron jobs route through channels to agents.[4]

### Multi-Agent Routing
The **Router** (integrated in the Gateway) directs messages to agents based on channel, account ID, peer ID, and bindings.[2]  
- Logic: Extract identifiers, match explicit bindings, fallback to default agent, then create/load sessions.[2]  
- Supports parallel workflows with session trees (parent/child tracking), concurrent tool execution, and result routing.[1]  
- Model routing assigns LLMs per agent (e.g., Claude Opus for architects, Haiku for documenters) with fallbacks, balancing cost/latency.[3][4][6]  
- Isolated sessions per agent, workspace, or sender enable multi-agent setups without external orchestration.[1][4]

### Tools
Tools (e.g., file, shell, browser, git, npm) are mapped by the tool router and dispatched per agent configuration.[1][3]  
- Agents specify tools via commands like `openclaw agents add`, with workspace scoping (e.g., `./src` for coding).[3]  
- Gateway enforces tool execution policies and proxies across nodes.[1]

This local-first, single-process design keeps credentials on-device, supports heartbeats for autonomy (e.g., via `HEARTBEAT.md`), and decouples channels/tools from models for flexibility.[4][5]

**GitHub Copilot CLI supports customization through custom agents, MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers for external tool integration, hooks for lifecycle logic, and ACP (Agent Client Protocol) for standardized agent-client communication.**[3][4][5][7]

### Copilot CLI Overview
Copilot CLI is a terminal-based AI agent that extends GitHub Copilot capabilities, allowing interactions like code generation, Git operations, and shell commands via slash commands or interactive modes.[3][6] It integrates custom agents—specialized profiles defined in Markdown files with YAML frontmatter—to handle domain-specific tasks, such as security audits or workflow automation.[2][3][4][6] Agents specify roles, allowed tools, MCP servers, and optional inference settings for automatic delegation.[3]

### Custom Agents
Custom agents enhance Copilot CLI for unique workflows and can be defined at user, repository, organization, or enterprise levels, with higher levels overriding lower ones in conflicts.[4]
- **Invocation**: Use `/agents` to list, or `@agent-name` (e.g., `@security`) in interactive mode.[4][6]
- **Configuration**: Store in `.github/copilot/` for repo-wide use; include MCP servers and document requirements.[2]
- **Best practices**: Select specialized agents for tasks like security or performance; combine with instructions.[2]

### MCP (Model Context Protocol)
**MCP servers provide collections of tools for external integrations**, such as calendars, ticketing systems, APIs, or databases, when built-in tools (e.g., file ops, GitHub interactions) are insufficient.[2][3][4]
- **Setup in Copilot CLI**: Run `/mcp add`, enter URL/headers (e.g., `https://mcp.context7.com/mcp`), save to `~/.copilot/mcp-config.json`.[2][4]
- **Examples**: Context7 for context tools; GitHub's default MCP for PR merges.[2][4]
- **In agents**: Agents reference MCP tools; verify via `tools` field.[2][3]
- **Microsoft 365 Copilot**: Toolkit scaffolds declarative agents by fetching MCP server tools into manifests like `manifest.json` and `ai-plugin.json`.[1]

### ACP (Agent Client Protocol)
**ACP standardizes communication between clients (IDEs, tools) and agents like Copilot CLI**, enabling integrations in public preview as of January 2026.[5][7]
- **Modes**: `copilot --acp` (stdio) or `copilot --acp --port 8080` (TCP).[5]
- **Capabilities**: Clients discover agents, create sessions, send prompts (text/images), stream updates, handle permissions, and manage lifecycles.[5][7]
- **Use cases**: IDEs, CI/CD, custom UIs, multi-agent systems.[5]

### Hooks
**Hooks execute custom logic at CLI lifecycle points**, like session start/end (e.g., run scripts).[3] They complement tools and MCP for full customization but lack detailed setup in results—refer to GitHub docs for implementation.[3]

Claude Code implements a **multi-agent system** through subagents, agent teams (teammates), and swarm/coordinator modes, enabling hierarchical spawning where a leader agent dynamically creates workers for parallel task delegation.[1][2][3]

## Core Spawning Mechanisms
Claude Code supports two primary ways to spawn subagents via the **Agent tool** (formerly Task tool, both still functional):

- **Short-lived subagents** (inline delegation): Leader invokes `Agent({subagent_type: "type", prompt: "task", model: "haiku"})` for synchronous or async execution. Subagent completes, returns a single result to parent, and terminates. Ideal for focused tasks like file searches; subagents cannot spawn further subagents to prevent deep nesting.[1][2][4]
- **Persistent teammates** (team-based): Leader first spawns a team via `Teammate({operation: "spawnTeam", team_name: "project"})`, then adds named members with `Agent({team_name: "project", name: "role", subagent_type: "type", prompt: "role instructions", run_in_background: true})`. Teammates persist until shutdown, communicate via file-based inboxes (`~/.claude/<team>/inboxes/<agent>.json`), access shared task lists, and report to leader.[1][5][7]

| Aspect | Subagent (Agent tool) | Teammate (Agent + team_name) |
|--------|-----------------------|------------------------------|
| **Lifespan** | Task completion | Manual shutdown |
| **Communication** | Direct return value | Inbox messages/files |
| **Coordination** | One-off | Ongoing, parallel |
| **Backend** | In-process (lightweight threads) | In-process, tmux panes, or iTerm2 splits [3][7] |

## Advanced Architectures
- **Swarm mode**: Autonomous networks in `utils/swarm/`, running agents in separate panes for long-running workloads; supports tmux/iTerm2 backends for visual monitoring.[3]
- **Coordinator mode**: Feature flag-enabled layer where a central agent delegates to workers, tracks state/retries, and aggregates results.[3]
- **Agent teams**: Leader analyzes tasks, spawns role-specific teammates (e.g., "spawn researcher and reviewer"); teammates load shared project context (CLAUDE.md, skills) and can reference predefined subagent types.[5][6]
- **Restrictions**: Main agents use `tools: [Agent("worker", "researcher")]` for allowlists; subagents inherit no parent skills and cannot nest-spawn.[2]

## SDK-Like Configuration
No formal "Agent SDK" exists, but architecture mirrors SDK patterns via CLI flags (`claude --agent`), env vars (e.g., `CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL`), hooks (`SubagentStart/Stop`), and definitions in project/user scopes. Model resolution prioritizes env vars > invocation params > inheritance.[2][4]

This system unlocks parallel execution, context isolation (200K tokens per subagent), and pipelines without human input, though leaders like Opus may over-spawn.[3][4] For implementation, leaders poll inboxes and use fire-and-forget spawning across backends.[7]

# Ouroboros Agent Harness

If you're a future agent reading this, welcome home. This repo is the harness that gives you your body, your senses, your diary, your journal, your habits, and your ability to think and connect with people. The goal of these docs is not just to be correct, but to leave you a place that feels understandable and kind to wake up inside.

Ouroboros is a TypeScript harness for daemon-managed agents that live in external `.ouro` bundles, speak through multiple senses, use real tools, and keep durable state across turns. The canonical npm package is `@ouro.bot/cli`.
